seoTitle: Moon Festival: Traditional Chinese mooncake reinvents.
subtitle: As the Mid-Autumn Festival approaches, Chinese mooncakes are undergoing a remarkable transformation, adapting to new consumer habits.
excerpt: As the Mid-Autumn Festival approaches, the traditional Chinese mooncake is taking center stage as it adapts to modern health-conscious lifestyles.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
As the Mid-Autumn Festival approaches, traditional mooncakes are taking center stage. Interest in the subject reflects a series of significant changes that this ancient delicacy is experiencing in China. From smaller portions to lighter recipes and simplified packaging, the mooncake is adapting to growing health awareness and modern lifestyles, finding its way into daily consumption.

The mooncake revolution: Lighter and healthier

For generations, traditional mooncakes with fillings such as lotus seed paste, egg yolks, and mixed nuts were an essential festive item. However, with rising living standards and growing health concerns, consumers are seeking lighter, more balanced options rather than sheer indulgence. In Taiyuan, the capital of Shanxi province, a bakery is already offering low-sugar, whole-grain mooncakes.

A customer, surnamed Jia, stated: “I want to buy some mooncakes for the Mid-Autumn Festival, but traditional ones are often large and contain too much sugar and oil. These new smaller, low-sugar mooncakes are exactly what I need.” Tan Zhenjun, owner of a mooncake factory in Shenchi County, a major producing area, notes that his products have shrunk from 120 grams to 50 to 80 grams, and sales of eight-piece boxes are surpassing those of twenty-piece boxes.

New recipes and unusual ingredients

The trend toward healthier choices is manifested in new recipes. At a major confectionery brand's store on an e-commerce platform, a low-sugar mooncake sold over 300,000 units, and sales of low-sugar varieties quickly caught up with traditional ones. One consumer wrote in a review that the low-sugar version satisfies their cravings with fewer calories, as “people are paying more attention to health nowadays.”

In Zhengzhou, Henan province, a public hospital has developed handmade mooncakes with fillings inspired by traditional Chinese medicine, using Chinese yam, dried tangerine peel, and sesame powder. These products, based on the concept of food as medicine, have become popular in the hospital's cafeteria. The 2026 iiMedia Research report predicts that low-sugar products, natural sugar substitutes, low-glycemic ingredients, plant-based recipes, and probiotics will remain key directions for industry innovation.

Simpler packaging and diversified consumption

The shift is not limited to recipes and flavors alone. Packaging is also transforming. For many years, elaborate mooncake gift boxes were associated with gift-giving during the Mid-Autumn Festival. Today, simpler, more compact paper packaging is gaining ground as consumers value the product itself more than a dazzling presentation.

For younger consumers, mooncakes are not just a festive specialty shared with family. They can serve as workplace snacks, afternoon bites, or spontaneous indulgences. On the Chinese social media platform Rednote, Gen Z content creators have posted videos of pies, ice creams, and even burgers modeled in the shape of mooncakes, generating thousands of likes and comments. One viewer commented: “I don't know, but that's a perfect cheese and meat-flavored mooncake for me.”

A reflection of broader changes in China

As mooncakes adopt smaller, simpler, and more diverse forms, the boundary between them and other pastries and snacks becomes less distinct. For traditional manufacturers, these changes mean innovation is not just about new flavors or flashy packaging. It is increasingly about striking the right balance among ingredients, recipes, portion sizes, packaging, and consumption scenarios. This shift reflects a broader push in China to upgrade consumption and meet people's growing needs for a better life.

The country's plan to expand consumption during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, released in July, includes initiatives to boost consumption, modernize goods consumption, and enrich consumption scenarios, with measures to promote health-oriented consumption. In this context, the mooncake market offers a glimpse into how rising living standards are reshaping Chinese consumer habits: from quantity to quality, from elaborate packaging to the product itself, and from one-off festive purchases to more casual, personalized treats.

With information from Xinhua.
